announced as part of the feed grains policy earlier in the session; and, of course, it is the intention of the government to carry out that undertaking. At least until July 31, 1948, the government has undertaken to pay the freight on all grains moving east for feeding purposes from Fort William. The freight, on grain moving to Fort William is, of course, taken care of in the price paid to farmers in the west. The freight is paid by the federal government from Fort William, east.
From 1943 until March 17 last there was a subsidy of ten cents a bushel paid on oats to the western farmer who produced oats, and a subsidy of fifteen cents a bushel to the western farmer who produced barley. On March 17 not only did we announce the continuation of the payment of freight, but in order to encourage the production of more barley we announced that the price of barley would be based on a floor of ninety cents for No. 1 feed barley. The intention was to have that apply when it was first proposed from August 1, on, in order to encourage the production of more barley in 1947. But we realized that, unless something was done further than that, no barley would be delivered until August 1, 1947. The farmer would simply hold it for a higher price. Therefore we announced that the higher price would come into effect that evening at midnight, and that all barley was then worth, not 64} cents, as it had been prior to that date, but that it was worth ninety cents, basis number one feed at Fort William. And having said that with regard to barley which was not yet delivered, we at the same time said that we would make provision for paying at the same rate all the farmers who had delivered barley during 1946-47. Provision was made for taking over the barley then in elevators, and making that policy effective.
In order to carry out our undertaking with the eastern farmer, in view of the fact that we had said to him that the ceiling price for his barley would be 64} cents during 1946^7, which we were under obligation to carry out down to August 1, 1947, we undertook to maintain the price to the eastern farmer at 64} cents down to August 1, but not beyond that date. This necessitated our paying out by way of subsidy considerably more than the fifteen cents we had previously paid out. We thought that would amount to about twenty-five cents a bushel, but in the process of carrying out the policy it actually amounted to about twenty-eight cents, so that we were paying out thirteen cents more than we paid prior to March 17, and wre now provide it as a drawback to the eastern producer rather

On two previous occasions in this house I have pointed out the danger to human beings from becoming affected with undulant fever, on account of using milk from infected herds of cows suffering from contagious abortion, Bang's disease. This disease is common, in all the provinces and affects human beings, and therefore undulant fever is common. As a physician it is only natural that I approach this question from the point of view of public health.
Undulant fever or Brucellosis is a disease which presents problems in control and diagnosis and treatment so far as human beings are concerned. To the dairy farmer, contagious abortion is an economic problem and seriously affects his livelihood. It might be of some interest to the committee to give a short outline of this disease.
In human beings undulant fever was first recognized during the Crimean war when the British army surgeons were unable to diagnose a strange fever which made its appearance among the troops. Undulant fever resembles several other diseases, and this made the diagnosis difficult in those days when it was rather hard to make a diagnosis without laboratory facilities; that is, they had no opportunity of making blood examinations. The British surgeons did not understand the disease because they had never seen it before. At the end of the year there were 8,000 sick men and only half the army was left fit to fight. Nothing further was discovered in the way of diagnosis until Doctor Bruce, a medical officer stationed on the island of Malta, discovered the bacterial cause of the disease. At that time it was called Malta fever. Doctor Bruce reported that the source of the disease was to be found in goat's milk. Goats are the main source of milk on the island of Malta. He discovered that by boiling the milk or pasteurizing it he was able to cut down the number of casualties to practically nil. Natives on the island of Malta who were still drinking the raw goat milk still continued to suffer, because half the goats on the island were infected.
The disease was introduced into the United States in 1905 through the importation of goats from Malta. A Danish research worker, Bernard Bang, discovered a microbe which causes contagious abortion in cattle, sometimes called Bang's disease. In 1918 a United States bacteriologist proved that Bang's disease of cattle and Malta fever, were caused from the same bacteria.
Undulant fever first appeared in Canada about 1929. It is now a fairly common disease, with a mortality of three per cent. Many cases, probably the majority, are not recognized, and are thought to be rheumatism, grippe, or influenza. Synovitis and arthritis, which we have been discussing on the estimates, are common symptoms, and it is necessary to make a diagnosis between undulant fever and infectious arthritis. Not all the cases are reported to the health authorities in Canada, but in one instance where 11,400 blood samples were examined, 600 samples showed the presence of undulant fever. Doctor Alice Evans, an authority on this disease, considers that about ten per cent of the rural population of the United States is affected. It is not a disease with a high mortality-I have already said it was three per cent-but it leaves a patient incapacitated from several weeks to two or three years, and it may leave permanent injury. Time may prove that it is one of the diseases responsible for rheumatic infections in human beings. Pasteurization is a preventive measure, but otherwise there is no cure for the disease. That is why I am concerned about the disease.
So far as cattle are concerned, Bang's disease has a high incidence in cattle throughout Canada. In 1945, among 2,713 herds tested, 905 showed a positive reaction to blood agglutination tests. This figure is taken from the report of the Department of Agriculture of Canada, 1945, at page 7. The loss to Canada's live stock can only be estimated. It has been stated that in Ontario, Bang's disease costs the farmers of this province alone over $20,000,000 annually. The United States department of agriculture has estimated a yearly loss of $80,000,000 for cattle, and $10,000,n00 for hogs.
To prevent Bang's disease in cattle, a vaccine containing the living Brucella has been produced. This vaccine has proven highly effective for immunization purposes. It is necessary that it be handled and administered only by trained workers. Careless handling of the vaccine, and exposure to extremes of heat and cold, spoil its efficiency. The disease is highly contagious in herds, and many owners are living in fear that valuable herds, built up over a period of years, may acquire the disease. Even if every care is used to protect a herd, there is still the danger of infection being carried to a clean herd by dogs, horses, hogs, dealers' trucks, or human beings. The value of Cotton's strain No. 19 lies m the fact that it produces immunity in a high percentage of the animals, and does not permit the disease to spread to susceptible animals.

I believe the department in Ottawa is on one side, some veterinarians on the other. However I shall just read what Dr. MacNabb of the Ontario veterinary college at Guelph has to say. This is what he says about calfhood vaccination:
1.	Build up a herd resistant to Bang's infection through calfhood vaccination.

2.	Vaccinate heifer calves at six to ten months of age. A veterinarian can procure the vaccine on application to the Ontario veterinary college.
3.	It is neither necessary nor of value to blood test the vaccinated calf thirty days following the calfhood vaccination procedure with strain 19 B. abortus.
4.	Note that without the practice of rigid sanitation, no control measure can be a success. It is inconceivable for any biological product- a vaccine or serum-to give the desired results in the absence of proper sanitary precautions.
5.	The vaccine used for calfhood vaccination purposes is a living suspension of strain number 19 B. abortus. Must be maintained at refrigeration temperature until used.
6.	Develops animal's resistance during early pregnancies.
7.	The only safe and effective method of establishing immunity in replacements for clean herds, so they will have a degree of resistance against exposure to the disease.
8.	A means of establishing a relative resistance of the cattle population when used as calfhood vaccination programme on an area basis.
9.	Calfhood vaccination will protect about 80 per cent of the animals for from three to five years. It will prevent the act of abortion in about 95 to 97 per cent of the vaccination animals.
10.	There is no evidence accumulated to date which would indicate the transmission of strain 19 B. abortus. Hence calfhood vaccination has been practised in blood negative Ontario governmental herds for the past seven years.
11.	No direct evidence has been shown that calfhood vaccination with strain 19 B. abortus induces sterility amongst the young vaccinates.
12.	Calfhood vaccination is best performed on young calves, dairy breeds at the age of six to nine months; beef breeds six to seven months.
13.	When abortion infection breaks in a herd, vaccination with strain 19 B. abortus at any age up to eighteen months is advisable. It should be borne in mind the older the calf or heifer when vaccinated the more pronounced will be the resistance. The blood will remain positive for varying periods of time in different individuals. Hence an animal vaccinated at twelve or fifteen months of age may be blood positive till it reaches thirty months of age.
14.	Calfhood vaccination on a community basis is a recommended procedure.
Then, I shall read what Doctor MacNabb has to say about adult vaccination. I brought this question up on two other occasions in the house. Of course the health cf animals branch does not agree with me, but I hope it will before many more years. With respect to adult vaccination he says this:
Not yet endorsed as a general routine control measure, adult vaccination lias, nevertheless, been practised; unfortunately, at times without merit. Adult vaccination is justified under certain conditions. The problem of control of contagious abortion is an individual herd problem. Adult vaccination is especially justified in herds where the abortion rate is high-as in the case of herds previously negative and suddenly exposed to infection. It is also justified in

It is a problem which arose in connection with a T.B. test made in the spring of 1946 which resulted in the slaughtering of the animals at the abattoir on May 15, 1946. It was a herd of Holstein cattle owned by a farmer named Donald McIntyre, on rural route Stayner, Ontario. He had a fully accredited herd of Holstein cattle and was engaged in the dairy business there in a very successful way. He had had for some ten years regular T.B. tests made of his herd, and during all that time none of his cattle had gone down in the tests or had reacted positively. But in the spring of 1946 no less than forty-four out of forty-four cattle in the herd reacted unfavourably to the T.B. test, and all went down. After this beneficial and enlightened discussion of cattle, I am going to change the subject to diseases of horses, nobler animals. We have good cattle in Bruce county but we also have good horses and good cabinet ministers. If any hon. members can come up to the Teeswater fall fair they will see that we have horses comparable with those at the royal winter fair in Toronto.
I am rising now to bring to the attention of hon. members the fact that there is a disease of horses which is not known to a great many. I did not know of it until the fall of 1946, when there was an outbreak in our township. That disease is called infectious anaemia; the nickname is swamp fever, and I think it also goes under about twelve other names. Learning of this outbreak in our township, and that the veterinary surgeon from the provincial department, Mr. Schofield, was there, I wrote the minister here in Ottawa. He was attending to some duties in the west, and in his absence I had a reply, part of which I should like to read:
While the loss to an individual owner may over a period of years, be considerable, there appears to be no tendency for the disease to spread to neighbouring premises. No regulations relating to swamp fever have been established, and the department has no authority to order diseased animals destroyed, or compensate the owner.
In this instance the outbreak of swamp fever meant the destroying of eight horses on one farm. The department at Guelph tried some different remedies which had not been tried before, including penicillin. The owner went to considerable expense, and found that no benefit was being derived. The result was that eventually he destroyed the horses which were infected.
I should like to give a few details I Obtained from a book called "Diseases of Horses," published by the United States department of agriculture. It says that

infectious anaemia was known in Europe as far back as 1843. Since 1900 it has been reported in twenty-nine of the forty-eight states of the United States of America. When a horse is affected with it he is incapable of regular work. Once a horse is infected, even if apparently it gets well, it is a carrier of the disease for life. The germ is transmitted by bloodsucking flies, and it has been reported that in a few instances in Europe men have been infected with the disease. The control depends upon the identification of the virus carriers. Up until now there has been no inoculation for the disease.
I should like to read some correspondence from veterinary surgeons with respect to this disease. The first letter is from Doctor A. L. MacNabb, principal of the Ontario veterinary college at Guelph. He writes:
Dear Dr. Robinson:
Dr. A. R. Campbell informed me that you were inquiring regarding swamp fever infection. As you know this is a condition long recognized; it is caused by an organism which is too small to be seen by the microscope and is transmissible from horse to horse. Age appears to make little difference.
The disease is transmitted by the exchange of horses during the incubative stage. This disease is not infrequent in the central west. There is every indication that it was introduced to the east from shipments of horses from these communities.
In your community I am informed eight horses either died or have been destroyed as a result of swamp fever infection. Dr. Schofield of our staff visited your community, and after postmortem examinations had been made the evidence points that the source of infection was due to the purchase in the fall of 1944 of a driving mare. The citizen who lost these horses was instructed by Dr. Schofield to disinfect the stables.
The eradication of the disease would take place much more quickly if the condition were a reportable one, the infected animals destroyed and the immediate contacts.
If there is any further information you desire in this connection we will be pleased to communicate with you.
Then I have'this further letter from one of our local veterinary surgeons:
In regard to swamp fever in horses I wish to say that I believe this disease should come under the contagious diseases act and when an animal is affected it should be disposed of and the owner paid for it and the remainder of horses quarantined for a length of time until one sees fit to release them.
And this is a letter from another veterinary surgeon in my district:
I understand that you are attempting to have swamp fever in horses dealt with under the contagious diseases act.
This is a move that would be very much in my favour, and I cannot express the necessity of having this disease more closely guarded.
In this territory in the last few years I have been in charge of several outbreaks, and of

,S apply-Ay ric u Uure
these, two were very costly, and not having authority to isolate these animals properly, and dispose of them properly, certainly gave the disease a very widespread area of infection.
Especially in a disease of this kind where diere is seemingly no treatment, and no apparent control measure, I believe it would be a very good measure to have it dealt with under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act.
I might also add that this disease has been recognized by our chief pathologist. The report of the science service of the Department of Agriculture for the year ended March 31, 1945 states, briefly:
Infectious anaemia of horses has continued to receive attention. A number of vaccines have been prepared but none of these has given encouraging results. For a time there was the suggestion that horses might be protected against the virus of infectious anaemia by inoculating another unrelated virus. The encouraging results in the early experiments have not been borne out.
And the 1946 report goes on to say:
Infectious anaemia - Further experiments directed towards the production of a vaccine were carried on. A crystal violet vaccine, prepared after the manner of swine fever vaccine, did not give rise to any immunity in susceptible horses. Intradermal inoculation of a very small dose of living virus did not produce infection, nor did it stimulate any immunity.
So, according to these science service reports, the disease is giving the chief pathologist some concern. I should be inclined to thnk it would be advisable for the minister to consider placing the disease under the contagious diseases act.
In connection with the local outbreak, may I say that the man who owned the horses deserved much credit. There was nothing to prevent his disposing of those horses to innocent people who would not knorv the animals were infected. The disease had been transmitted to his horses through a driving mare which he had purchased in 1944 and which had come originally from western Canada.
I should be inclined to think that in the event of an outbreak there should be some regulation whereby the disease would become reportable and animals "linically showing symptoms would be immediately destroyed and the owner recompensed for the loss. Probably other ones not showing clinical symptoms could be quarantined, or whatever measures are considered necessary could be taken.
May I point out that the book to which I have referred says there is no way of testing a horse to find out if it is infected with the disease, other than by the process of drawing blood from one horse w'hich it is believed is infected and injecting it into a horse which it is known is not infected, and then watching the results on the uninfected horse. So that whatever conclusion the department arrives at will not be an easy one; they are so much in the dark about the disease at the present time. However I would be inclined to think the minister's department would be well advised to look into the matter to see what can be done in an effort to stamp out this disease.

I should like to answer what has been just said with regard to this matter. It is true that swamp fever in horses is prevalent in some parts of the west, and there is a possibility that horses shipped from there have brought the disease along with them. The departmental officials are of the opinion that one of the conditions which brings about swamp fever is faulty sanitary conditions, inadequate or improperly balanced rations, exceptionally hot weather or other debilitating influences which react unfavourably on the animal. No specific diagnostic tests for swamp fever have yet been found. Mercurial chloride tests, while not specific, may be of some value as an aid in the diagnosis of swamp fever. Although swamp fever has engaged the efforts of many workers, no means of prevention or specific cures have resulted1 from their studies. Practising veterinarians employ certain treatments using a number of preparations, especially sodium cacodylate; rest, an abundance of good feed, good sanitary environment and the elimination of all influences that are debilitating in character constitute the best known means of combating the ravages of swamp fever.
As to the suggestion that they should be put in the same class as animals suffering from T.B., that there may be difficulties in that. One can understand why it would be helpful to persons who have animals suffering from that disease, but that is the situation. It is not so general as T.B. Another point which has not been raised tonight, is the compensation paid for animals that are condemned when you set up a T.B.-free area. The compensation of $38 a head might have been all right in the days referred to by the minister when we got next to nothing for our cattle. It was about half the price, but today it represents only about one-fifth of what an animal is worth. When we have an animal that reacts and has to go out of the herd it costs us anything from $150 to $200 to replace it. I am referring to the ordinary good grade of milch cow.
If this compensation is not raised I know that farmers are going to be reluctant to let this test go on. The last time I spoke in the house and drew the attention of the minister to this matter, some hon. member said that $96 was paid for purebred animals. That is all right, but we do not all have purebred animals. The average dairy man today is working with grade animals, and I am sure the minister knows that. Compensation of $38 is not sufficient for an animal that is condemned.
When I sit down the minister may say that the farmer has the benefit of the beef as well, which brings quite a good price today.
